'''''Thapsia villosa''''', commonly known as the '''villous deadly carrot''', is a [[species]] of [[poisonous plant|poisonous]] [[herb]]aceous [[plant]]s in the [[genus]] ''[[Thapsia (plant)|Thapsia]]''. It grows to about {{convert|70|to|190|cm|in|abbr=on}} in height. It has [[pinnate]] hairy leaves with sheath-like [[petiole (botany)|petioles]]. The flowers are yellow in color and borne on compound [[umbel]]s. They develop into fruits with four wings characteristic of the genus. It is native to southwestern [[Europe]] and northwestern [[Africa]] surrounding the [[Mediterranean Sea]]. The plant was used extensively for [[traditional medicine]] since around the 3rd century BC.

==Taxonomy==
''Thapsia villosa'' was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' (1753).<ref name="eumed">{{cite web|url=http://ww2.bgbm.org/EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=107962&PTRefFk=7500000|title=''Thapsia villosa'' L.|publisher=Euro+Med Plantbase, Botanic Garden and Botanical Museum Berlin-Dahlem|access-date=August 26, 2012}}</ref> It is classified under the [[genus]] ''[[Thapsia (plant)|Thapsia]]'', [[subfamily]] [[Apioideae]], of the [[carrot]] and [[parsley]] [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Apiaceae]].<ref name="GRIN">{{GRIN| name = ''Thapsia villosa'' L.| id = 310966| accessdate =August 26, 2012}}</ref> Two [[Variety (botany)|varieties]] are recognized: ''T. villosa'' var. ''villosa'' and ''T. villosa'' var. ''dissecta''.<ref name="iberica"/>

The [[genus|generic name]] ''Thapsia'' is derived from the [[Ancient Greek]] name θαψία (''thapsía'') for the members of the genus. The Greeks believe it to have originated from ancient [[Thapsos]] in [[Sicily]]. The [[specific epithet (botany)|specific epithet]] is from [[Latin]] ''[[wikt:villosus|villōsus]]'' ("hairy" or "shaggy").<ref name="iberica"/><ref name="ichn"/>

It is commonly known in English as the '[[wikt:villous|villous]] deadly carrot' or simply 'deadly carrot'.<ref name="partington">{{cite book|editor =Charles Frederick Partington|editor-link =Charles Frederick Partington|title =The British Cyclopædia of Natural History|publisher =Orr & Smith|year =1835–1837|page=243|url =https://archive.org/download/britishcyclopd02partrich/britishcyclopd02partrich.pdf}}</ref><ref name="donn">{{cite book|author=James Donn|title =Hortus cantabrigiensis: or, A catalogue of plants, indigenous and foreign, cultivated in the Walkerian botanic garden, Cambridge|publisher =John Burges|year =1800|page=34|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=F5cCAAAAYAAJ&pg=RA1-PT36}}</ref> It is known under a large number of common names in other languages, including ''bu-nefar'' in [[Arabic language|Arabic]]; ''zumillo'' and ''cañaheja'' in [[Spanish language|Spanish]]; ''baladra'' in [[Catalan language|Catalan]]; ''croca'' in [[Majorcan language|Majorcan]]; ''turbit-da-terra'' in [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]]; ''bermidor'' in [[Basque language|Basque]]; ''turbith bâtard'' in [[French language|French]]; and ''turbito falso'' in [[Italian language|Italian]].<ref name="eumed"/><ref name="brun">{{cite book|author=Franco Brunello|editor =Neri Pozza|title =The Art of Dyeing in the History of Mankind|publisher =Vicenza|year =1973|page=390–391|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=MI-vbcXDdssC&pg=PA390}}</ref>

==Description==
''Thapsia villosa'' is a [[perennial]] [[herb]] growing to a height of {{convert|70|to|190|cm|in|abbr=on}}. It has a robust and smooth tapering [[Plant stem|stem]] about {{convert|5|to|25|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter, arising from a thick root resembling a white [[carrot]] or [[turnip]].<ref name="ichn"/><ref name="mt"/>
[[File:Thapsia villosa StemandLeavesPuertollano.jpg|thumb|left|180px|[[Pinnate]] leaves and sheath-like [[petiole (botany)|petioles]] of ''T. villosa'']]
The leaves, like the name of the species suggests, are hairy. The leaves around the base of the stem have well-developed sheath-like [[petiole (botany)|petiole]]s about {{convert|20|to|80|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide. Like the leaves, they are also hairy. They are whitish, yellowish, green, or (rarely) purple in color. The leaf blades are triangular to deltoid in shape and are [[pinnate]], subdivided once to thrice. The last [[leaflet (botany)|leaflet]] subdivision is usually about {{convert|8|to|32|mm|abbr=on}} wide in ''T. villosa'' var. ''villosa''; while they are only about {{convert|1.5|to|3|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide in ''T. villosa'' var. ''dissecta''.<ref name="iberica"/> The margins of the leaves are curled ([[Glossary of botanical terms#R|revolute]]) with small teeth-like and triangular serrated edges, each tipped with small spike. The main leaf [[midrib]] ([[rachis]]) is densely covered in hair and light to dark green on the upper side, while it is smooth and grayish to greenish on the underside.<ref name="iberica">{{cite book|language=Spanish|editor =S. Castroviejo|title =Flora Iberica. Volume X: Araliaceae-Umbelliferae|publisher =Real Jardín Botánico|year =2003|pages=401–410|isbn =978-8400081508 |url =http://www.floraiberica.es/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/10_129_83%20Thapsia.pdf|display-editors=etal}}</ref> The leaves are largest at the bottom and progressively become smaller the higher they are on the stem.<ref name="mt"/> In the upper parts of the stem, the leaves are often reduced to nothing more than petioles which form sheaths around the stem.<ref name="lindley">{{cite book|author=John Lindley|title =Flora medica; a botanical account of all the more important plants used in medicine, in different parts of the world.|publisher =Longman, Orme, Brown, Green, and Longmans|year =1838|page=52|url =http://biodiversityheritagelibrary.org/page/17801527#page/72/mode/1up}}</ref>

Like other members of the genus, the [[inflorescence]] of ''Thapsia villosa'' is a compound subhemispherical to globose [[umbel]]. It has 9 to 29 spokes and is about {{convert|6|to|12|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter. [[Bract]]s are usually absent, though in rare cases, one to three may be present, each around {{convert|6|to|40|mm|in|abbr=on}} in length and lanceolate in shape. The [[umbellule]]s are hemispherical to globose. [[Bracteole]]s are also usually absent, though rarely 1 or 2 may be present. Each umbellule has about 18 to 43 flowers, each with five bright yellow elliptical petals. The fruits are oblong and around {{convert|9|to|15|mm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|6|to|11|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide. When mature, they are light to dark brown in color with four yellowish to brownish wings characteristic of the genus.<ref name="iberica"/><ref name="mt"/><ref name="lindley"/> The main umbel has [[Hermaphrodite (botany)|hermaphroditic]] flowers, containing both [[stamen]] and [[pistil]]. Smaller umbels may develop from the sides of the stem which usually contains only [[stamen]]s. These umbels wither away quickly.<ref name="ichn"/>

''Thapsia villosa'' is highly variable in morphology. The two varieties, ''T. villosa'' var. ''dissecta'' and ''T. villosa'' var. ''villosa'' are usually distinguished by how many times the leaf subdivides into leaflets. ''T. villosa'' var. ''dissecta'' has leaves that are deeply subdivided two or three times into narrow and small leaflets. ''T. villosa'' var. ''villosa'', in contrast are usually subdivided only once or twice. However, there are numerous intermediate forms between the two varieties and distinguishing between them can be very difficult. The [[diploid chromosome number]] (2n) of ''Thapsia villosa'' is 22, 33, 44, or 66.<ref name="iberica"/>

==Ecology==
[[File:Thapsia villosa InflorescenceCloseupPuertollano.jpg|thumb|Flowers of an [[umbellule]] of ''Thapsia villosa'']]
[[File:Matera Thapsia Villosa 11-05-2022 13-30-04.jpg|thumb|''Thapsia villosa'' in [[Matera]], Italy]]
Unlike most members of the family Apiaceae, ''Thapsia villosa'' flowers early, during the months of May, June, and July. The flowers are [[pollinated]] by a variety of [[insect]]s. The flowers develop into winged fruits that dry out around August, while other members of the family are usually still in bloom.<ref name="ichn"/><ref name="mt"/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Thapsia villosa habitusPuertollano.jpg|thumb|''Thapsia villosa'' in bloom in [[Puertollano]], [[Spain]]]]
The native range of ''Thapsia villosa'' extends from southern [[France]] and the [[Iberian Peninsula]] ([[Spain]], [[Portugal]], and [[Gibraltar]]) to northwestern [[Africa]] ([[Morocco]], [[Algeria]], and [[Tunisia]]). It has also been introduced into [[Corsica]].<ref name="iberica"/><ref name="calpensis">{{cite book|author=Edward Frederick Kelaart|title =Flora calpensis; contributions to the botany and topography of Gibraltar, and its neighbourhood|publisher =J. van Voorst|year =1846|page=109|url =http://biodiversityheritagelibrary.org/page/24019301#page/141/mode/1up}}</ref> They can be found growing at altitudes of {{convert|0|to|1800|m|ft|abbr=on}} [[above sea level]] in [[scrubland]]s, clearings, and near [[Ruderal species|recently disturbed land]] like roads or cultivated fields.<ref name="iberica"/>

In its native range, it is frequently confused with the similar-looking ''[[Ferula communis]]'', the giant fennel. ''Thapsia villosa'' and ''Ferula communis'' share some common names in Spanish like ''cañaheja''.<ref name="ichn">{{cite web|url=http://ichn.iec.cat/bages/brolles/Imatges%20grans/cThapsia%20villosa.htm|language=Spanish|title=El zumillo (''Thapsia villosa'')|publisher=Institució Catalana d’Història Natural|access-date=August 30, 2012|archive-date=July 4, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160704195716/http://ichn.iec.cat/Bages/brolles/Imatges%20grans/cThapsia%20villosa.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> Reports of ''Thapsia villosa'' in the [[Balearic Isles]] is likely the result of confusion with ''[[Thapsia gymnesica]]''.<ref name="iberica"/>

==Toxicity==
''Thapsia villosa'' is highly [[poisonous]].<ref name="fda">{{cite web|url=http://www.herbvideos.com/Poisos.htm|title=Poisonous Plant Database (Plant List): Vascular Plant List|author=D. Jesse Wagstaff|publisher=Center for Food Safety & Applied Nutrition, U.S. Food & Drug Administration|access-date=August 30, 2012|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120311173803/http://www.herbvideos.com/Poisos.htm|archivedate=March 11, 2012}}</ref><ref name="pammel">{{cite book|author =Louis Hermann Pammel|title =A manual of poisonous plants, chiefly of eastern North America, with brief notes on economic and medicinal plants, and numerous illustrations|publisher =The Torch Press|year =1911|page =857|url =http://biodiversityheritagelibrary.org/page/37822045#page/747/mode/1up|archive-date =2013-04-14|access-date =2012-08-26|archive-url =https://archive.today/20130414112656/http://biodiversityheritagelibrary.org/page/37822045%23page/747/mode/1up#page/747/mode/1up|url-status =dead}}</ref> Skin contact with the roots can cause severe itching and swelling.<ref name="mt"/><ref name="grieve"/>

==Uses==

===Traditional medicine===
The medicinal properties of the members of the genus ''[[Thapsia (plant)|Thapsia]]'' were recognized as early 300 BC.<ref name="srik">{{cite journal|author1=Adusumilli Srikrishna|author2=K. Anebouselvy|name-list-style=amp|year=2003|title=Enantiospecific first total synthesis of (+)-''cis,anti,cis''-3-hydroxy-1,8,12,12-tetramethyl-4-oxatricyclo(6.4.0.0<sup>2,6</sup>)-dodecan-9-yl senecioate, the optical antipode of a natural thapsane isolated from ''Thapsia villosa''|journal=Tetrahedron Letters|volume=44|issue=5|pages=1031–1034|url=http://144.206.159.178/ft/1010/85923/1452338.pdf|doi=10.1016/s0040-4039(02)02733-8|url-status=dead}}</ref> In [[traditional medicine]], the roots of ''Thapsia villosa'' were used as a [[purgative]] and [[emetic]]. [[Resin]] from the ''Thapsia villosa'' was used as a [[blister agent|blister-producing agent]] (vesicant) or a [[counterirritant]], similar to resin derived from ''[[Thapsia garganica]]''.<ref name="grieve">{{cite web|url=http://botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/t/thapsi10.html|title=Thapsia|author=M. Grieve|publisher=Botanical.com|access-date=August 26, 2012}}</ref><ref name="gould">{{cite book|author= George Milbry Gould|title =An illustrated dictionary of medicine, biology and allied sciences|publisher =P. Blakiston's Son|year =1907|page=1509|url =http://www.biodiversityheritagelibrary.org/page/23278672#page/1523/mode/1up}}</ref> In [[Spain]], the resin is also traditionally used in [[Segarra]] as treatment for [[scabies]].<ref name="iberica"/> [[Poultice]]s made from root bark infused with oil was used as a pain-reliever and for treating [[rheumatism]]. These were also used in [[Salamanca (province)|Salamanca]] for treating cracks in [[Horse hoof|horse hooves]].<ref name="mt"/>

Traditional medicinal uses of the plant, however, are now considered largely ineffective and highly inadvisable due to the danger posed by the poisons of ''Thapsia villosa''.<ref name="ichn"/><ref name="mt">{{cite web|url=http://www.mtplantas.com/eng/plants/E38522.htm|title=Zumillo (''Thapsia villosa'')|publisher=MundoTema |access-date=August 30, 2012}}</ref><ref name="smc">{{cite web|url=http://www.sonremedioscaseros.com/zumillo/|title=Zumillo|language=Spanish|publisher=Son Remedios Caseros|access-date=August 30, 2012}}</ref>

===Medical research===
Along with ''[[Thapsia garganica]]'' and ''[[Thapsia transtagana]]'', ''Thapsia villosa'' var. ''villosa'' contains C-19 [[terpenoid|terpenolide]]s  with strong [[SERCA]]-inhibiting properties ''[[in vitro]]''. They are of interest to medical researchers for their potential in treating [[neurodegenerative disorder]]s like [[Alzheimer's disease|Alzheimer's]] or [[Parkinson's disease]].<ref name="Alkhamisi">{{cite book|author=Riham Alkhamisi|title =A new approach towards the synthesis of Transtaganolides/Basiliolides – C-19 Terpenolides from Thapsia with SERCA-inhibiting activity|publisher =Lunds Tekniska Högskola|year =2011|url =http://lup.lub.lu.se/luur/download?func=downloadFile&recordOId=2204317&fileOId=2204323}}</ref>

=== Other uses ===
Poison from the roots of ''Thapsia villosa'' is traditionally used by fishermen in [[Catalonia]] as an [[ichthyotoxin]] for [[Fish toxins|stunning fish]], making them easier to catch.<ref name="mt"/><ref name="arias">{{cite journal|author=Beatriz Teresa Álvarez Arias|year=2000|title=Ichthyotoxic plants used in Spain|journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology|volume=73|issue=3|pages=505–512|doi=10.1016/S0378-8741(00)00336-6|pmid=11091006}}</ref> Extracts from the root bark of ''Thapsia villosa'' have been used since ancient times as a yellow [[dye]].<ref name="brun"/> In the 18th century, yellow dye from the flowers were used to color [[wool]].<ref name="brun"/><ref name="salis">{{cite book|author=William Salisbury|title =The Botanist's Companion. Volume 2|publisher =R. and A. Taylor|year =1816|page=129|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=l_EYAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA135}}</ref> ''Thapsia villosa'' are also grown as [[ornamental plant|ornamentals]] for their bright yellow flowers.<ref name="barr">{{cite journal|author1=Lurdes Barrico |author2=Anabela Marisa Azul |author3=Maria Cristina Morais |author4=António Pereira Coutinho |author5=Helena Freitas |author6=Paula Castro  |name-list-style=amp |year=2012|title=Biodiversity in urban ecosystems: Plants and macromycetes as indicators for conservation planning in the city of Coimbra (Portugal)|journal=Landscape and Urban Planning|volume=106|issue=1|pages=88–102|doi=10.1016/j.landurbplan.2012.02.011|url=http://www.eko.uj.edu.pl/laskowski/Seminarium/Materialy/LUP2012_Barrico.pdf}}</ref>
